paras: The threatened lynching of Andrew Beal followed the killing of Henry Speers, a white locomotive engineer, at Franklin, Missouri, on Christmas Eve 1880, when Beal, a young Black man, was accused of cutting Speers's throat with a razor. Parties of citizens hunted Beal, and newspapers called his pursuers a lynching party. No report of his capture or fate appears in the coverage.

Franklin was a small railroad town a few miles out from St. Louis on the Missouri Pacific Road, and Speers was one of that road's engineers. According to a St. Louis dispatch, the whole town celebrated Christmas Eve "in a lively way," and several fights took place that night.

After words with Speers, Beal was said to have drawn a razor and slashed him; Speers called for help and tried vainly to draw a revolver. Beal fled out of town into the brush and, the night being dark, escaped. Speers was carried into a grocery store with his jugular vein severed and cuts across the windpipe, and he died a little after 1 a.m. on December 25.

On Christmas Day parties of citizens scoured the woods for Beal, who was thought to be hiding nearby, and the dispatch remarked that if he were caught "it is probable that no one will ever find out what became of him." The St. Louis chief of police received a telegram describing Beal as about 20 years old, five feet seven inches tall, with a smooth face.
No report of Beal's capture, lynching or trial, or of an inquest on Speers, was found.

The Chicago Daily Tribune carried the only full account, a special St. Louis dispatch headlined "MURDERED BY A NEGRO" that called Beal "the darky" and "the fugitive murderer" and treated a lynching as the likely end without objection. A one-sentence digest of the story ran in Wisconsin weeklies, in the Wood County Reporter on December 30 and in the River Falls Journal's crime column on January 6, 1881. That brief said Beal fled toward St. Louis "followed by a competent lynching party."

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Andrew Beal
bases: After Beal was accused of killing Speers, citizens hunted him through the woods and a digest called his pursuers 'a competent lynching party', but no paper reports that he was caught or harmed (A1, A3).

Parties of citizens pursued Beal over the killing of Speers, and the papers called them a 'lynching party' and implied he would vanish if caught (A1, A3), but no report of his capture, death or fate was found, so a killing cannot be established.

The St. Louis dispatch in the Chicago Tribune (A1) is the only full report; the identical Wisconsin briefs (A2, A3) read as a news-digest condensation of the same wire story rather than an independent account.

accounts.label: St. Louis dispatch
accounts.gist: After several fights in a town celebrating Christmas Eve, Beal and Speers exchanged words; Beal drew a razor and cut Speers's throat while Speers tried to draw a revolver, then fled into the brush; citizens were scouring the woods and the dispatch suggested no one would learn his fate if he were caught.

accounts.label: News-digest brief
accounts.gist: After a Christmas Eve fight at Franklin, Beal killed Speers with a razor and fled toward St. Louis, 'followed by a competent lynching party'.

framing.detail: The Tribune's 'MURDERED BY A NEGRO' headline and terms like 'the darky' present Beal's guilt as fact, and it reports the likely lynching matter-of-factly without condemning it.
Wisconsin weeklies ran a one-sentence crime-column brief calling the pursuers 'a competent lynching party'.

versions.value: Fled out of town into the brush and was supposed to be hiding in the vicinity
Fled in the direction of St. Louis

conflicts.note: Minor; the Tribune also says St. Louis police would likely capture him if he came to the city, and the fuller St. Louis dispatch is the better evidence for where the search was made.
